The name translates to 'eleven leaves' (or eleven elements), referencing the goal of gathering cards from a central area. Players use cards from their hand to 'scoop' cards of matching rank or sum from the table, known as the 'Palette'. It is played in both competitive 'Professional' and casual 'Amateur' formats, with the professional game featuring the strict 'Yoruba Rules' that forbid duplicate cards in a single capture.
Dates from the slave trade era, rooted in Yoruba culture of Nigeria, West Africa. Evolved into a card-based game during the colonial period and remains popular in Nigeria in the 21st century.
2 to 5 players. Professional games use 2 players; amateur games use 3-4.
Standard 52-card deck. Four special cards are removed: King, Queen, Jack, and 9 of Diamonds, placed face-up on the table as the initial palette.
Standard 52-card deck. Four special cards are removed: King, Queen, Jack, and 9 of Diamonds, placed face-up on the table as the initial palette.
Each player receives 4 cards to start. Rounds continue until the deck is exhausted.

items.text: Professional Rules: Strict competition format: 3 rounds per game, no jokers used, applies Yoruba Rules strictly (no duplicate cards in captures), non-playing dealer as referee.
Amateur Rules: Casual play format: 4 rounds per game, jokers (2 additional cards) may be used, Normal Rules apply (duplicates allowed in captures), more relaxed penalties.

Esun (Building): Optional rule: Players can combine played card with table cards into protected piles that only they can later scoop. Pile must be scooped before next deal, otherwise player is penalized.
Isiwo (Card Viewing): Optional rule: Players may look through their own scooped cards at any time to track what cards remain in deck. Opponents' cards cannot be viewed.
